1.translation: Arjuna said: Out of kindness toward me you have spoken the supreme secret, the teaching known as the knowledge of the Self, and through those words this delusion of mine has departed.
1.nuances: Sivananda, Gambirananda and Adidevananda keep adhyātma as a secret 'concerning the Self', Sankaranarayan expands it into 'a science governing the Soul', and Prabhupada generalises it to 'confidential spiritual subjects' and renders the delusion as 'illusion'; Purohit alone speaks of 'illusions which surrounded me' in the plural.

2.translation: For I have heard from you in full detail how beings arise and pass away, O lotus-eyed one, and I have heard also of your imperishable greatness.
2.nuances: All take bhavāpyayau as the origin and dissolution of beings; Gambirananda adds a bracketed gloss that these happen 'in You', Adidevananda replaces the epithet 'lotus-eyed' with 'O Krsna', and Prabhupada shifts 'heard' to 'realized' for the second half and speaks of 'living entities'.

3.translation: It is just as you have described yourself, O supreme Lord. Yet I long to see your sovereign form, O best of persons.
3.nuances: Sivananda, Gambirananda, Adidevananda and Sankaranarayan read the first line as a simple assent to Krishna's self-description, with aiśvara rendered 'divine' or 'Lordly'; Purohit turns it into a confession of belief, while Prabhupada expands the request into wanting to see how Krishna 'entered into this cosmic manifestation'.

4.translation: If you think it possible for me to see it, O Lord, then, master of yoga, show me your imperishable Self.
4.nuances: The address yogeśvara is 'Lord of the Yogins' (Sivananda, Sankaranarayan), 'Lord of Yoga' (Gambirananda, Adidevananda), 'Lord of Lords' (Purohit) or 'master of all mystic power' (Prabhupada); ātmānam avyayam is 'imperishable/eternal Self' for most, 'Yourself completely' for Adidevananda and 'unlimited universal Self' for Prabhupada.

5.translation: The Blessed Lord said: Behold, Pārtha, my forms by the hundreds and by the thousands, of many kinds, divine, in many colours and shapes.
5.nuances: All agree on hundreds and thousands of divine forms in varied colours and shapes; Prabhupada alone frames them as 'My opulences', and the translators differ only in whether to keep 'son of Pṛthā' (Gambirananda, Sankaranarayan, Prabhupada) or substitute 'Arjuna'.

6.translation: See the Ādityas, the Vasus, the Rudras, the two Aśvins and the Maruts. See many wonders never seen before, Bhārata.
6.nuances: Sivananda, Gambirananda, Adidevananda, Sankaranarayan and Prabhupada keep the proper names of the deity groups, whereas Purohit replaces them with allegorical 'Powers of Nature' such as fire, earth and wind; Sankaranarayan renders bhārata as 'son of Pandu' and Prabhupada as 'best of the Bhāratas', and Prabhupada adds 'or heard of'.

7.translation: Here, today, behold the entire universe, moving and unmoving, gathered as one within my body, Guḍākeśa, together with anything else you wish to see.
7.nuances: All agree that the whole universe stands together in one place in Krishna's body; Gambirananda and Sankaranarayan retain the epithet Guḍākeśa, the others say 'Arjuna', and Prabhupada expands the final clause into a promise covering whatever Arjuna may wish to see 'in the future'.

8.translation: But you cannot see me with this ordinary eye of yours. I give you a divine eye: behold my sovereign yoga.
8.nuances: Yoga aiśvara is kept as 'lordly/divine Yoga' by Sivananda, Gambirananda and Adidevananda, concretised as 'Lordly form' by Sankaranarayan, 'glory of My Sovereignty' by Purohit and 'mystic opulence' by Prabhupada; Prabhupada and Purohit pluralise 'eyes' while the rest keep the single divine eye.

9.translation: Sañjaya said: Having spoken thus, O king, Hari, the great master of yoga, revealed to Pārtha his supreme sovereign form.
9.nuances: Sivananda, Gambirananda and Sankaranarayan retain 'Hari', Adidevananda and Purohit write Krishna, and Prabhupada 'the Personality of Godhead'; Purohit's 'Almighty Prince of Wisdom' for mahāyogeśvara is idiosyncratic, and Prabhupada labels the form 'universal form' where others keep 'supreme Lordly/divine form'.

10.translation: A form with many mouths and eyes, with many wondrous sights, with many divine ornaments and many divine weapons held aloft.
10.nuances: All translators list mouths, eyes, wonders, ornaments and raised weapons; Prabhupada and Purohit convert the descriptive compound into a narrative sentence about what Arjuna saw, and Purohit adds 'flaming' to the weapons.

11.translation: Wearing divine garlands and garments, anointed with divine perfumes, made wholly of wonder, radiant, infinite, with faces turned in every direction.
11.nuances: Viśvatomukha is 'faces on all sides' for Sivananda, Gambirananda, Adidevananda and Sankaranarayan, 'Omnipresent' for Purohit and 'all-expanding' for Prabhupada; Sankaranarayan alone specifies the unguent as sandal paste and offers 'godly' as an alternative for deva.

12.translation: If the light of a thousand suns were to rise in the sky all at once, that might resemble the radiance of that great being.
12.nuances: Most keep the simile as a possible likeness, but Purohit says a thousand suns would be only 'a faint reflection', Sankaranarayan turns it into a rhetorical question, and Prabhupada inflates the number to 'hundreds of thousands of suns' and names the subject 'the Supreme Person in that universal form'.

13.translation: There, in the body of the God of gods, the son of Pāṇḍu then saw the entire universe standing as one, yet divided in countless ways.
13.nuances: All agree the universe appears unified in one place yet manifold; Sivananda and Sankaranarayan speak of 'many groups', Adidevananda of 'manifold divisions', and Prabhupada paraphrases into 'unlimited expansions of the universe ... divided into many, many thousands'.

14.translation: Then Dhanañjaya, filled with wonder, his hair standing on end, bowed his head to the god and spoke with his palms joined.
14.nuances: Sivananda, Gambirananda, Adidevananda and Sankaranarayan render vismaya as wonder or amazement, Purohit as being 'dumb with awe', and Prabhupada as 'bewildered and astonished', adding that Arjuna 'began to pray'; Gambirananda and Sankaranarayan keep the epithet Dhanañjaya.

15.translation: Arjuna said: I see within your body, O god, all the gods and the many hosts of beings, Brahmā the Lord seated on the lotus, all the seers and the divine serpents.
15.nuances: Sivananda, Gambirananda and Sankaranarayan read brahmāṇam īśam as Brahmā the ruler on his lotus seat, whereas Adidevananda and Prabhupada take īśa as a separate reference to Śiva; Purohit paraphrases the gods as 'powers of Nature' and serpents as 'shining angels'.

16.translation: I see you with countless arms, bellies, mouths and eyes, of boundless form on every side; I see no end, no middle and no beginning of you, Lord of the universe, universal form.
16.nuances: All translators agree on the list of limbs and the absence of beginning, middle and end; Purohit softens the anatomy to 'faces, eyes and limbs', while the others keep arms, bellies, mouths and eyes, and all keep the twin address 'Lord of the universe, universal form'.

17.translation: I see you crowned, bearing mace and discus, a mass of brilliance blazing on every side, hard to look upon, shining all around like blazing fire and sun, immeasurable.
17.nuances: Sankaranarayan alone pluralises 'crowns, clubs and discs' and Prabhupada follows him with 'various crowns, clubs and discs'; Purohit replaces the mace with a 'sceptre', and the rest keep diadem, mace and discus in the singular.

18.translation: You are the imperishable, the supreme object of knowledge; you are the ultimate resting place of this universe; you are the undecaying guardian of the eternal dharma; you are, I hold, the everlasting Person.
18.nuances: Śāśvata-dharma is 'eternal Dharma/law' for Sivananda, Adidevananda and Prabhupada, 'ever-existing religion' for Gambirananda, 'Life Eternal' for Purohit, and Sankaranarayan uniquely reads it as 'the pious act of the Satvatas'; nidhāna is treasure-house (Sivananda, Purohit), repository (Gambirananda), substratum (Adidevananda) or resting place (Sankaranarayan, Prabhupada).

19.translation: I see you without beginning, middle or end, of infinite power, with endless arms, the moon and sun for your eyes, your mouth a blazing sacrificial fire, scorching this universe with your own radiance.
19.nuances: Vīrya is 'power' (Sivananda, Purohit, Adidevananda), 'valour' (Gambirananda), 'creative power' (Sankaranarayan) or 'glory' (Prabhupada); Purohit reads hutāśa as 'fire of sacrifice' and softens the burning to 'flooding with light', while Prabhupada intensifies it to fire 'coming forth from Your mouth, burning this entire universe'.

20.translation: This space between heaven and earth and all the directions are filled by you alone; seeing this wondrous and terrible form of yours, O great soul, the three worlds tremble.
20.nuances: All agree that Krishna alone pervades the interspace and the quarters, and that the three worlds are frightened; Prabhupada modernises lokatraya as 'all the planetary systems', and Sankaranarayan omits 'terrible' from the description of the form.

21.translation: These hosts of gods enter into you; some, afraid, praise you with joined palms. Crying 'Hail!', the throngs of great seers and siddhas extol you with abundant hymns.
21.nuances: Puṣkala is 'complete' (Sivananda), 'elaborate' (Gambirananda), 'meaningful' (Adidevananda) or 'excellent' (Sankaranarayan); Prabhupada adds that the gods are 'surrendering' and that the hymns are Vedic, and renders svasti as 'All peace!' where others have 'Hail' or 'may it be well'.

22.translation: The Rudras, Ādityas, Vasus and Sādhyas, the Viśvedevas, the two Aśvins, the Maruts and the ancestors who drink the steam of offerings, the hosts of gandharvas, yakṣas, asuras and siddhas all gaze upon you in astonishment.
22.nuances: Ūṣmapāḥ is glossed as 'the manes' or 'forefathers' by most and literally 'Steam-drinkers' by Sankaranarayan; Purohit allegorises the whole list into natural forces and 'Mammon-worshippers', and Prabhupada reads 'Rudras' as 'manifestations of Lord Śiva' and siddhas as 'perfected demigods'.

23.translation: Seeing your vast form with its many mouths and eyes, O mighty-armed one, its many arms, thighs and feet, its many bellies and its terrible many fangs, the worlds are shaken, and so am I.
23.nuances: Lokāḥ is 'the worlds' for Sivananda, Purohit, Adidevananda and Sankaranarayan, 'the creatures' for Gambirananda and 'all the planets with their demigods' for Prabhupada; Sankaranarayan reads daṃṣṭrā as 'tusks' where the others say 'teeth' or 'jaws'.

24.translation: Seeing you touch the sky, blazing with many colours, your mouths gaping, your great eyes aflame, my inmost self trembles, and I find neither steadiness nor peace, O Viṣṇu.
24.nuances: Adidevananda reads nabhas as 'the Supreme Heaven' rather than the sky; dhṛti is 'courage' (Sivananda, Purohit, Sankaranarayan), 'steadiness' (Gambirananda, Prabhupada) or 'support' (Adidevananda); Prabhupada adds the epithet 'all-pervading' to Viṣṇu while Purohit drops the name entirely.

25.translation: Having seen your mouths terrible with fangs, like the fire at the end of time, I lose all sense of direction and find no refuge. Be gracious, Lord of gods, dwelling-place of the universe.
25.nuances: Kālānala is 'fires of cosmic dissolution' (Sivananda, Gambirananda, Purohit), 'fire of final destruction' (Adidevananda, Sankaranarayan) or simply 'deathlike' (Prabhupada); all keep the plea for mercy, and Prabhupada moves it to the front and paraphrases losing direction as 'I cannot keep my balance'.

26.translation: And all these sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, together with the hosts of kings, Bhīṣma, Droṇa and that son of the charioteer, along with the chief warriors on our side as well,
26.nuances: Most leave the verse incomplete as a run-on into 27, but Gambirananda supplies 'enter into You' and Prabhupada folds in the whole of 27, including heads smashed between the teeth; Sankaranarayan is the only one to render sūtaputra literally as 'son of the charioteer' rather than naming Karṇa outright.

27.translation: rush headlong into your mouths, gaping with terrible fangs. Some are seen caught between your teeth, their heads crushed to powder.
27.nuances: Sivananda, Gambirananda, Adidevananda and Sankaranarayan all keep the image of heads crushed between the teeth, Purohit heightens it to 'crushed to atoms', while Prabhupada's entry here is actually his rendering of verse 29 (the moth simile), having absorbed the content of 27 into verse 26.

28.translation: As the many torrents of rivers race toward the sea alone, so these heroes of the human world pour into your blazing mouths.
28.nuances: All agree on the river-to-ocean simile; Sankaranarayan is most literal with 'water-rapids' and 'the ocean alone', Purohit dramatises 'rivers in flood surge furiously', and Prabhupada replaces 'heroes of the world of men' with 'great warriors'.

29.translation: As moths plunge with quickening speed into a burning flame to their destruction, so too do the worlds rush with quickening speed into your mouths to be destroyed.
29.nuances: Lokāḥ is 'creatures' (Sivananda, Gambirananda), 'men' (Purohit, Adidevananda), 'worlds' (Sankaranarayan) or 'all people' (Prabhupada); all keep the moth simile and the sense of self-destruction, which Purohit phrases as 'court their own destruction'.

30.translation: You lick your lips as you devour all the worlds on every side with your flaming mouths; your fierce rays fill the entire universe with brilliance and scorch it, O Viṣṇu.
30.nuances: Lelihyase is rendered literally as licking by Sivananda, Adidevananda, Sankaranarayan and Gambirananda ('lick Your lips'), while Purohit paraphrases 'lap them in flame' and Prabhupada drops it; Gambirananda alone omits the vocative Viṣṇu, and Prabhupada says 'all people' where others say 'worlds'.

31.translation: Tell me who you are in this fierce form. I bow to you, best of gods; be gracious. I wish to understand you, the primal one, for I do not comprehend what you are doing.
31.nuances: Pravṛtti is 'working' (Sivananda), 'actions' (Gambirananda), 'activity' (Adidevananda), 'behaviour' (Sankaranarayan), 'what Thou intendest' (Purohit) or 'mission' (Prabhupada); Purohit also reads ādyam as a request to see Krishna 'as Thou wert at first' rather than as the epithet 'primal One'.

32.translation: The Blessed Lord said: I am Time, destroyer of worlds, grown mighty, and I have set out here to annihilate the worlds. Even without you, none of the warriors drawn up in the opposing ranks will survive.
32.nuances: Sivananda, Gambirananda, Adidevananda and Prabhupada render kāla as 'Time', while Purohit says 'the Destroyer' and Sankaranarayan attaches pravṛddha to the worlds ('overgrown') rather than to Time; Prabhupada reads ṛte 'pi tvām as excepting the Pāṇḍavas and says soldiers 'on both sides', whereas the rest say the warriors of the hostile armies will die even without Arjuna's action.

33.translation: Therefore rise up and win glory; conquer your enemies and enjoy a prosperous kingdom. I have already slain them; be merely the instrument, Savyasācin.
33.nuances: All agree that the enemies are already slain by Krishna and Arjuna is a mere instrument; Sankaranarayan says 'token cause' and glosses Savyasācin as 'ambidextrous archer', Adidevananda as 'great bowman', and Prabhupada adds 'by My arrangement' and 'in the fight'.

34.translation: Droṇa, Bhīṣma, Jayadratha, Karṇa and the other warrior-heroes have already been slain by me: strike them down, do not be distressed. Fight, and you will defeat your rivals in battle.
34.nuances: Mayā hatān is 'already slain by Me' for Sivananda, Gambirananda, Sankaranarayan and Prabhupada, but 'condemned' (Purohit) and 'doomed' (Adidevananda); all agree on the command to fight without distress and the promise of victory.

35.translation: Sañjaya said: Having heard these words of Keśava, the diademed Arjuna, trembling and with palms joined, bowed and spoke again to Kṛṣṇa, his voice faltering, prostrate and overcome with fear.
35.nuances: Kirīṭī is kept as an epithet by Gambirananda and glossed 'crowned-prince' by Sankaranarayan, while the others simply say Arjuna; Prabhupada adds 'O King' and 'to Dhṛtarāṣṭra' and makes the bowing 'again and again', and Purohit renders bhītabhīta as 'awe' rather than fear.

36.translation: Arjuna said: Rightly, Hṛṣīkeśa, does the world rejoice and delight in your praise; the rākṣasas flee in terror in every direction, and all the hosts of siddhas bow before you.
36.nuances: Sthāne is 'meet', 'proper', 'rightly' or 'appropriate' across the translators, with Purohit's 'natural'; anurajyate is 'rejoices' for most but 'attracted' (Gambirananda), 'love' (Adidevananda) and 'attached to You' (Prabhupada); Sankaranarayan glosses Hṛṣīkeśa as 'Lord of sense-organs' and Prabhupada 'master of the senses'.

37.translation: And why should they not bow to you, great soul, who are greater even than Brahmā, the first creator? Infinite one, Lord of gods, dwelling-place of the universe, you are the imperishable, being and non-being, and that which lies beyond both.
37.nuances: Sankaranarayan and Purohit read the comparison as Krishna being greater than Brahmā, while Sivananda, Gambirananda and Adidevananda make Krishna the first creator even of Brahmā; Adidevananda, following Rāmānuja, takes akṣara as 'the imperishable individual self', and Prabhupada replaces sat-asat with 'the invincible source, the cause of all causes, transcendental to this material manifestation'.

38.translation: You are the first of gods, the ancient Person; you are the supreme resting place of this universe. You are the knower and what is to be known, and the highest abode; by you, O being of infinite form, the universe is pervaded.
38.nuances: Dhāma is 'Abode' for most and 'Final Home' for Purohit, which Prabhupada expands to 'supreme refuge, above the material modes'; Sankaranarayan attaches 'infinite forms' to the universe rather than to Krishna as a vocative, and Prabhupada reads vettā as 'knower of everything'.

39.translation: You are Vāyu, Yama, Agni, Varuṇa, the moon; you are Prajāpati and the great-grandfather of all. Homage, homage to you a thousand times, and again and yet again homage, homage to you.
39.nuances: Sivananda, Adidevananda and Sankaranarayan keep the Sanskrit names, Gambirananda and Purohit translate them (Air, Death, Fire, the god of the waters), and Prabhupada renders Yama as 'supreme controller' and Prajāpati as 'Brahmā, the first living creature'; Purohit alone writes 'Father and Grandfather' for Prajāpati and prapitāmaha.

40.translation: Homage to you from before and from behind, homage to you from every side, O All! You of endless might and measureless power, you pervade everything, and therefore you are everything.
40.nuances: Gambirananda reads purastāt as 'in the East' rather than 'in front'; vikrama is 'prowess', 'heroism', 'powers', 'majesty' or 'might' depending on the translator, and all agree on the closing inference that because Krishna pervades all he is all.

41.translation: Whatever I said rashly, thinking you a mere friend, calling you 'Kṛṣṇa', 'Yādava', 'friend', not knowing this greatness of yours, whether through carelessness or out of affection,
41.nuances: Sivananda, Purohit, Gambirananda, Adidevananda and Sankaranarayan all read the verse as Arjuna's apology for over-familiar address, differing only in whether prasabham is 'presumptuously', 'rashly', 'rudely' or 'importunately'; Prabhupada's entry in the source data is a misplaced repeat of verse 33 and does not render this verse.

42.translation: and whatever disrespect I showed you in jest, while at play, resting, sitting or eating, whether alone or in front of others, Acyuta, for all that I beg your forgiveness, immeasurable one.
42.nuances: Tat-samakṣam is 'in company' or 'in public' for Sivananda, Purohit, Gambirananda and Adidevananda, but Sankaranarayan specifies 'in the presence of respectable persons'; aprameya is 'immeasurable', 'incomprehensible' or 'without an equal' (Purohit), and Prabhupada's entry in the source is a stray verse from chapter 10, so he offers no rendering here.

43.translation: You are the father of the world of moving and unmoving things; you are its object of worship and its venerable teacher, greater than any. There is none equal to you, so how could there be anyone greater, in all three worlds, O being of matchless power?
43.nuances: Guru garīyān is 'greatest Guru' (Sivananda), 'Teacher, and greater than a teacher' (Gambirananda), 'Master of Masters' (Purohit) or 'supreme spiritual master' (Prabhupada); Prabhupada adds that no one 'can be one with You', a doctrinal insertion absent from the Sanskrit and from the other translators.

44.translation: So, bowing down and laying my body prostrate, I seek your grace, O Lord worthy of praise. As a father bears with a son, a friend with a friend, a lover with the beloved, so should you bear with me, O god.
44.nuances: Priyaḥ priyāyai is 'lover and beloved' for Sivananda, Purohit and Gambirananda, Adidevananda reads it as mutual dearness between Krishna and Arjuna, Sankaranarayan drops it, and Prabhupada makes it 'a husband the familiarity of his wife'; soḍhum is 'forgive' for some and 'bear with' or 'tolerate' for others.

45.translation: I rejoice at having seen what was never seen before, yet my mind is shaken with fear. Show me that other form of yours, O god; be gracious, Lord of gods, dwelling-place of the universe.
45.nuances: Tad eva rūpam is understood as the previous or usual form by Sivananda, Purohit and Sankaranarayan, 'that very form' by Gambirananda, 'Your other form' by Adidevananda, and Prabhupada explicitly names it 'Your form as the Personality of Godhead'.

46.translation: I wish to see you just as before, crowned, with mace and discus in hand. Take on that same four-armed form, O thousand-armed one, O universal form.
46.nuances: All agree Arjuna asks for the four-armed form with crown, mace and discus; Purohit again substitutes 'sceptre' for the mace, and Prabhupada adds the conch and lotus not mentioned in the Sanskrit and renders kirīṭin as 'helmeted'.

47.translation: The Blessed Lord said: By my grace, Arjuna, this supreme form of mine has been shown to you through my own yoga: radiant, universal, infinite, primal, which no one but you has ever seen before.
47.nuances: Ātmayogāt is 'My own Yogic power' (Sivananda, Gambirananda), 'My own free will' (Adidevananda), 'My internal potency' (Prabhupada), while Sankaranarayan uniquely reads it as the result of Arjuna's own concentration on the Self; Prabhupada adds 'within the material world'.

48.translation: Not by study of the Vedas or sacrifices, not by gifts, not by rituals, not by fierce austerities can I be seen in this form in the world of men by anyone but you, great hero of the Kurus.
48.nuances: Vedayajñādhyayana is split variously as 'study of the Vedas and sacrifices' (Sivananda, Gambirananda, Prabhupada) or expanded into three items by Adidevananda; Gambirananda adds a gloss restricting it to those without grace, and Prabhupada renders kriyā as 'pious activities' and nṛloka as 'the material world'.

49.translation: Do not be distressed or bewildered at having seen this terrible form of mine. Free of fear and glad at heart, behold once more that familiar form of mine.
49.nuances: Tad eva rūpam idam is 'former form' (Sivananda), 'earlier form' (Gambirananda), 'usual Form' (Purohit), 'other form' (Adidevananda) or 'the same as before' (Sankaranarayan); Prabhupada paraphrases freely, addressing Arjuna as 'My devotee' and offering 'the form you desire'.

50.translation: Sañjaya said: Having spoken thus to Arjuna, Vāsudeva showed his own form once more; the great soul, becoming gentle in body again, reassured the frightened one.
50.nuances: Svakaṃ rūpam is 'His own form' for most, 'accustomed form' for Purohit and, oddly, 'tiny form' for Sankaranarayan; Prabhupada reads the verse as a two-stage return, first to the four-armed and then to the two-armed form, which no other translator finds in the Sanskrit.

51.translation: Arjuna said: Seeing this gentle human form of yours, Janārdana, I have now regained my composure and returned to my natural state.
51.nuances: Saumya is 'gentle' for most, 'pleasing' for Adidevananda and 'so very beautiful' for Prabhupada; sacetāḥ is 'composed', 'calm' or Sankaranarayan's 'collected my thinking faculty', and Prabhupada adds a narrative frame calling this Krishna's 'original form'.

52.translation: The Blessed Lord said: This form of mine that you have seen is exceedingly hard to behold; even the gods forever long to see it.
52.nuances: All agree the form is extremely hard to see and that the gods perpetually desire it; Purohit alone says 'the most powerful have longed for it in vain', and Prabhupada adds 'which is so dear' and reads the form as the one Arjuna is seeing now.

53.translation: Not by the Vedas, nor by austerity, nor by gifts, nor by sacrifice can I be seen in this way, as you have seen me.
53.nuances: Sivananda, Gambirananda, Adidevananda and Sankaranarayan render the four means literally, Purohit generalises 'the Vedas' to 'the scriptures', and Prabhupada rewrites 'seen' as 'understood' and adds 'with your transcendental eyes' and 'as I am'.

54.translation: But by undivided devotion, Arjuna, I can be known in this way, truly seen, and entered into, O scorcher of foes.
54.nuances: Ananyā bhakti is 'single-minded' (Sivananda, Gambirananda, Adidevananda), 'undeviating' (Sankaranarayan), 'tireless' (Purohit) or 'undivided devotional service' (Prabhupada); praveṣṭum is 'entered into' for most, 'become one with Me' for Purohit, and 'enter into the mysteries of My understanding' for Prabhupada.

55.translation: Whoever acts for my sake, holds me as the highest, is devoted to me, free of attachment and without hostility toward any being, that one comes to me, son of Pāṇḍu.
55.nuances: All agree on the five marks of the devotee who attains Krishna; Prabhupada expands saṅgavarjita into freedom from 'fruitive activities and mental speculation' and turns 'without enmity' into 'friendly to every living being', while Purohit renders Pāṇḍava as 'My dearest son'.

56.translation: Oṁ, that is the real. Thus ends the eleventh chapter, entitled The Yoga of the Vision of the Universal Form, in the glorious Bhagavad Gītā, the Upaniṣads, the knowledge of Brahman, the scripture of yoga, the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Arjuna.
